Transcript: Earthquake waves are how we see inside the planet. Nobody has drilled more than about twelve kilometers down, but every large earthquake sends waves through the whole Earth, and stations on the far side record them. By the early twentieth century, seismologists had noticed something odd. Beyond roughly a hundred and four degrees around the globe from an earthquake, the direct waves went quiet. There was a band, a shadow zone, where stations picked up very little, and then, farther out, strong arrivals again. The explanation was a core, about twenty-nine hundred kilometers down, that bends waves sharply, the way a lens bends light. And since one kind of wave, the shear wave, can't travel through liquid and never came through the core, most researchers concluded the core was liquid.

So the picture seemed settled: a molten core, with a shadow behind it. Then in 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann published a paper with what may be the shortest title in the field, just P-prime. She'd been studying records of a large earthquake in New Zealand, and she noticed weak waves arriving inside the shadow zone, where, on the accepted model, they had no business being. Others had tended to explain such arrivals away. Lehmann took them seriously. She showed they made sense if there were a second boundary, deeper down, an inner core where the waves travel faster and get bent back toward the surface.

Now, here's what usually gets lost in the retelling. Lehmann didn't prove the inner core was solid. Her argument was about speed, not state. The idea that it's solid came a few years later, and firm evidence took until the early 1970s, from the way the whole planet rings like a bell after a great earthquake. What she did was refuse to treat inconvenient data as junk.

Transcript: In English, and in most languages that have been studied, the future is in front of you and the past is behind. We look forward to the weekend; we put a bad year behind us. Cognitive linguists, building on work by George Lakoff and Mark Johnson around 1980, argue that metaphors like these aren't decoration. We understand an abstract domain, time, through a concrete one, space.

So it's striking that Aymara, a language spoken in the Andes, seems to reverse it. The Aymara word for front, which is also the word for eye, is used for the past, and the word for back is used for the future. A reasonable skeptic might say, so what? Languages are full of dead metaphors. English speakers say breakfast without ever thinking about breaking a fast. Maybe the Aymara words are just fossils, and nobody actually pictures the past in front of them.

To test that, the cognitive scientist Rafael Núñez and the linguist Eve Sweetser looked not at words but at hands. In a study published in 2006, they recorded Aymara speakers talking about earlier and later events and analyzed their spontaneous gestures. Older speakers, especially those who spoke little Spanish, pointed or swept forward when talking about the past, and gestured backward, over the shoulder, for what was to come. Younger speakers fluent in Spanish tended to gesture the Spanish way. People don't usually plan their gestures, so this is hard to dismiss as a figure of speech.

And the logic behind the reversed layout makes sense once you see it. The past is what you've already seen, so it lies before your eyes. The future can't be seen, so it's behind you. The idea that we think of time through space held up. What turned out to vary was which feature of space a culture builds it on.

item.correct_answer: Aymara speakers really do locate the past in front
item.explanation: Gesture evidence shows the reversed mapping is more than a dead metaphor.

Transcript: You've probably met this claim: Jan van Eyck invented oil painting. It goes back to Giorgio Vasari, the sixteenth-century Italian writer whose biographies of artists still shape how we tell this period. In Vasari's version, van Eyck, working in Flanders in the early fourteen hundreds, was experimenting with varnishes, hit on oil as a binder for his pigments, and the secret eventually made its way to Italy.

It's a tidy story, and in that form it's wrong. Painters had been mixing pigments with oil for centuries. A monk known as Theophilus, writing a craft manual in the twelfth century, describes it, and he also complains about it. Each layer, he says, has to dry before you add the next, and with some colors that takes a very long time, so it's tedious for pictures. That was the real obstacle. It just wasn't practical for detailed painting.

So what did van Eyck do? Two things, as far as studies can tell. First, he seems to have prepared his oils so they dried faster, which made a slow, layered process workable. Second, he exploited something that tempera, the egg-based paint most painters used, does far less well: translucent layers. He'd lay down an opaque base, then build thin, tinted films of oil paint over it. Those are glazes. Light passes through those films, bounces off the bright white ground underneath, and comes back out. That's where the glow of the jewels and fabrics in a work like the Ghent Altarpiece, finished in 1432, comes from.

And notice the irony. The property Theophilus grumbled about, that oil paint has to be built up in separate layers, is exactly what van Eyck turned into a method. People long searched his paintings for a secret ingredient. The analyses mostly turned up ordinary drying oils. The secret, if there was one, was in the handling.

To argue that Theophilus was the first painter to use oil

item.explanation: The lecture rejects Vasari's 'invented oil painting' claim and explains faster drying and glazing.

It goes back to Giorgio Vasari, the sixteenth-century Italian writer whose biographies of artists still shape how we tell this period. In Vasari's version, van Eyck, working in Flanders in the early fourteen hundreds, was experimenting with varnishes, hit on oil as a binder for his pigments, and the secret eventually made its way to Italy.

It's a tidy story, and in that form it's wrong. Painters had been mixing pigments with oil for centuries. A monk known as Theophilus, writing a craft manual in the twelfth century, describes it, and he also complains about it. Each layer, he says, has to dry before you add the next, and with some colors that takes a very long time, so it's tedious for pictures. That was the real obstacle. It just wasn't practical for detailed painting.

So what did van Eyck do? Two things, as far as studies can tell. First, he seems to have prepared his oils so they dried faster, which made a slow, layered process workable. Second, he exploited something that tempera, the egg-based paint most painters used, does far less well: translucent layers. He'd lay down an opaque base, then build thin, tinted films of oil paint over it. Those are glazes. Light passes through those films, bounces off the bright white ground underneath, and comes back out. That's where the glow of the jewels and fabrics in a work like the Ghent Altarpiece, finished in 1432, comes from.

And notice the irony. The property Theophilus grumbled about, that oil paint has to be built up in separate layers, is exactly what van Eyck turned into a method. People long searched his paintings for a secret ingredient. The analyses mostly turned up ordinary drying oils. The secret, if there was one, was in the handling.

Transcript: Most soils in the Amazon basin are, frankly, poor for farming. That surprises people, because the forest above them is so lush. But in a warm, wet climate, soils have been weathered for a very long time, rain washes the nutrients out, and most of the nutrients there are sit in the living plants, not in the ground. Clear the forest, farm for a few years, and yields usually drop.

And yet, scattered through the region, often on bluffs near rivers, there are patches of dark, rich soil, sometimes a meter or more deep, that people still dig up and even sell as potting soil. In Portuguese it's called terra preta, black earth. Some researchers once assumed it formed naturally, maybe from volcanic ash or old lake beds. But these soils are full of broken pottery. They're human-made, built up over centuries of settlement, and many seem to be well over a thousand years old.

What makes them black is charcoal. Ordinary plant matter rots away within a few years in that climate, but charcoal can last for centuries, and its porous surface holds on to nutrients that would otherwise wash out. That finding set off a wave of enthusiasm for what's now called biochar. The idea is that charcoal worked into fields can recreate Amazonian fertility and lock away carbon too.

Here's the problem. Terra preta isn't just charcoal. It's charcoal mixed with fish and animal bones, ash, manure, and household waste, added little by little over generations. When researchers add charcoal alone to soil, the results vary widely, from clear gains to almost nothing, depending on the soil and the crop. Charcoal seems to be what holds the nutrients in place. It isn't what supplied them. Whether the residents meant to improve the soil, or were just piling up rubbish, is still debated.

Transcript: In the early 1950s, Japanese researchers studying a troop of macaques on the small island of Koshima began leaving sweet potatoes on the beach, to draw the monkeys into the open. In 1953 a young female the researchers called Imo did something new. She carried a sandy potato to a stream and washed it. Over the next few years the habit spread, and later the troop took to washing potatoes in the sea, perhaps for the salty taste.

You may have heard a far more dramatic version. In a popular book from the late 1970s, a writer claimed that once a certain number of monkeys, say the hundredth, had learned to wash potatoes, the habit suddenly jumped to every monkey on the island, and even to troops on other islands, with no contact at all. That's the hundredth monkey story, and there's no evidence for it. The writer later conceded that it rested on very little.

The real record is more interesting. The habit spread slowly, over years, and along social lines. One of Imo's playmates and her mother picked it up first, then her siblings and other young monkeys. Infants learned it from their mothers. Most of the adult males never took it up at all. That pattern looks like learning by watching companions, which is why Koshima became an early example of what some call animal culture.

Not everyone accepts that label. The psychologist Bennett Galef pointed out that the spread was slow, as if each monkey had partly worked it out alone. He also noted that the researchers were feeding the monkeys, which could have encouraged the behavior. Now, I'm not sure he's right. But his is the right kind of challenge. It's an argument about how the habit spread, built from the same records. The hundredth monkey story asked us to ignore them.

Transcript: For centuries, sailors could find their latitude fairly easily, from the height of the Sun or the Pole Star. Longitude, how far east or west you were, was the hard problem. The Earth turns fifteen degrees an hour, so if you know the time at your home port and the local time where you are, the difference gives you your longitude. Local time you can get from the Sun. The trouble was carrying home-port time across an ocean, because the best clocks of the day, pendulum clocks, couldn't keep time on a rolling ship.

In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds for a practical solution. John Harrison, a largely self-taught clockmaker, spent decades building sea clocks, and his fourth, a large pocket watch, did remarkably well on test voyages to the Caribbean in the 1760s. Yet the Board of Longitude paid him only part of the prize. He got substantial money later only after appealing to Parliament, with support from King George the Third.

The popular telling, popularized by a 1990s bestseller, casts this as a lone genius against snobbish astronomers, especially Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, who backed a rival method. That method, lunar distances, worked out home-port time by measuring the Moon's position against the stars and using printed tables. There's some truth to the snobbery charge. But the Board's demand wasn't absurd. One extraordinary watch isn't a method. They wanted proof that other makers could copy it, and they could. A copy by Larcum Kendall sailed with James Cook on his second Pacific voyage and performed very well.

Even then, chronometers were expensive, and for decades many ships relied on lunar tables, published yearly by Maskelyne, often checking one method against the other. The watch won in the end. But the astronomers' caution wasn't only prejudice.

Transcript: There's an old idea, going back at least to the nineteenth century, that forests act like sponges. They soak up the rain and let it out slowly, so if you cut down a forest, the streams below it will dry up. It's intuitive, and it shaped land policy in several countries.

The way hydrologists tested it is called a paired catchment experiment. You find two small neighboring watersheds with similar soils, slopes, and rainfall, and you measure the streams draining both for several years, so you know how they compare. Then you cut the trees in one and keep the other as a control. At Hubbard Brook, in New Hampshire, in the mid-1960s, researchers cleared all the forest in one small watershed and used herbicides to stop it growing back. The result went the opposite way from the sponge idea. Streamflow went up, by something like forty percent in the first year.

The reason is transpiration. Trees pull water out of the soil and release it into the air through their leaves, and a forest does that over an enormous surface. Take the trees away, and more of the rain ends up in the stream. A review in the early 1980s, pooling dozens of these experiments, found the same direction almost every time, with the biggest effects where evergreen conifers were removed.

So, case closed against the sponge? Not everywhere. In tropical cloud forests on mountain slopes, the trees comb droplets right out of passing fog, water that would never have fallen as rain. Clear those forests, and streams can lose water.

Transcript: In the summer of 1954, the psychologist Muzafer Sherif and his team ran one of the best-known field studies in social psychology, at a summer camp in Robbers Cave State Park in Oklahoma. Twenty-two boys, about eleven years old, were split into two groups that at first didn't know the other existed. Each group bonded and chose a name, the Rattlers and the Eagles. Then the staff, who were really researchers, set up a tournament with prizes, and hostility followed fast: name-calling, a burned flag, raids on each other's cabins.

The next phase is the part textbooks emphasize. Simply bringing the groups together, for meals or movies, didn't help. The shared meals turned into food fights. What did help were what Sherif called superordinate goals, problems neither group could solve alone, like a broken water supply, or a stalled truck that needed everyone pulling on a rope. Over several of these, the hostility faded.

Here's what the textbooks usually leave out. The year before, in 1953, Sherif ran a similar study near Middle Grove, New York, and it fell apart. According to later accounts, including archival work by the writer Gina Perry, the boys there kept friendships across the two groups and didn't turn on each other as planned, and at one point some of them seem to have suspected that the staff were behind the incidents meant to provoke them. The study was abandoned and largely left out of the published record.

Now, that doesn't mean the Robbers Cave findings were faked. But it changes how we should read them. Competition for prizes didn't produce hostility automatically. In 1954, the groups were kept apart from the very beginning. The conflict grew under conditions the researchers had arranged quite carefully, and those conditions probably mattered more than the textbook version suggests.

Transcript: Ludwig van Beethoven was one of the first major composers to tell us exactly how fast he wanted his music played. In 1815, the inventor Johann Maelzel patented a practical metronome, a clockwork pendulum with a sliding weight. Move the weight up or down, and the ticking slows down or speeds up. Beethoven was enthusiastic. In 1817, he published metronome markings for his first eight symphonies: numbers, instead of loose Italian words like allegro.

And for two hundred years, performers have argued with those numbers. Many of them are startlingly fast. Some passages, played at the marked speed, feel rushed, almost frantic, and most orchestras have quietly taken them slower.

So people looked for an explanation. Beethoven was going deaf. Or his metronome was faulty, an early mechanism running unevenly. But a broken machine ought to produce errors that go every which way: some markings too fast, some too slow, by differing amounts.

In 2020, two researchers in Spain tried another approach. They measured the tempos in dozens of recorded performances of the symphonies and compared them with Beethoven's markings. The conductors weren't scattered at random. They were slower by a fairly steady amount, roughly twelve beats a minute. And the researchers pointed out that this is about what you'd get if someone read the scale on the wrong side of the sliding weight, the bottom edge instead of the top. That's a human slip, not a mechanical fault, and it could have been made by Beethoven or by someone helping him, since he couldn't hear the ticking well.

Now, that's a hypothesis, not proof. But notice what it does to the old debate, which was always framed as whether to trust Beethoven or not. If the error was systematic, his markings may still tell us the speeds he intended, once you correct for it.

Transcript: For centuries, Chinese porcelain was one of the most prized things you could buy in Europe. It was white and hard, thin enough to let light through, and it rang when you tapped it. European potters couldn't make anything like it, and they didn't know why. Even the name shows how little they understood. Porcelain comes from an Italian word for a kind of cowrie shell, because the material seemed to resemble one, and some writers guessed it was actually made from crushed shells.

Europeans did produce imitations. In Florence, in the late fifteen hundreds, workshops backed by the Medici family made what we now call soft-paste porcelain, and French factories later made more. They mixed clay with ground glass. The result looked something like the real thing, but it was softer, easier to scratch, and liable to slump or crack in the kiln.

The breakthrough came in Saxony, in eastern Germany, around 1708. Johann Friedrich Böttger was an alchemist, kept under guard by the ruler, Augustus the Strong, who wanted him to make gold. He worked with an older scholar, Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus, who had been reaching very high temperatures with huge burning lenses. By testing local clays and minerals methodically, they found the answer, and it wasn't a hidden technique. It was the ingredients: a white clay called kaolin, plus a mineral that helps it fuse, fired at around thirteen hundred degrees or more, far hotter than ordinary European kilns. The Meissen factory opened in 1710.

Now, Böttger usually gets the credit. But Tschirnhaus died in 1708, just as the work came together, and some historians think his notes and his approach did much of the work. And look again at what the Medici imitators had been doing. They copied how porcelain looked. The real problem was what it was made of.

Transcript: You may have heard that the largest living thing on Earth is a fungus. In the Malheur National Forest in Oregon, there's a honey fungus, a species of Armillaria, that's been estimated to cover close to a thousand hectares, and to be anywhere from about two thousand to more than eight thousand years old. Headlines call it the humongous fungus.

What you see above ground isn't much: clusters of honey-colored mushrooms in the autumn. The fungus itself is mostly underground and inside wood, a mass of fine threads plus dark, rootlike cords that grow through the soil from one tree root to the next. It's a parasite, and it kills many of the trees it spreads through, which is how researchers first noticed the pattern, as patches of dead and dying conifers.

So how do you know it's one organism and not many? The method goes back to a study published in 1992 on a related fungus in Michigan. Researchers took samples across a large area and compared them genetically, and they kept finding the same individual. In Oregon, a team did the same thing, and samples spread across several kilometers matched.

But here's where we have to be careful about what that evidence shows. Matching genes tell you the samples came from one individual that grew outward from a single beginning. They don't tell you it's all still connected. Over centuries, the cords between distant patches may have died, leaving genetically identical pieces that no longer exchange anything. Is that one organism, or a clone colony? The genetic test can't decide.

So the record is real, as a record of how far one genetic individual has spread. Whether it's the largest organism depends on what you mean by organism, and the people who study fungi don't entirely agree on that.

Transcript: Ask who invented printing with movable metal type, and most people will say Johannes Gutenberg, around 1450. But the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is Korean. It's called the Jikji, a collection of Buddhist teachings printed at a temple in Cheongju in 1377, roughly seventy-five years before Gutenberg's Bible. Only its second volume survives, and it's held by the national library of France. And movable type itself goes back further still, to the Chinese printer Bi Sheng, who made type from baked clay in the eleventh century.

So why didn't printing in Korea set off the kind of explosion it did in Europe? The usual answer is the writing system. Korean scholars wrote in Chinese characters, which number in the thousands, so a printer needed an enormous stock of type. Compare that with a couple of dozen letters in the Latin alphabet.

There's something to that, but it runs into a problem. In 1443, King Sejong's court created hangul, the Korean alphabet, which also has only a couple of dozen letters. And Korean printers did cast hangul type. Yet printing didn't take off in the European way after that, either.

Many historians now point instead to who was doing the printing, and why. In Korea, metal type was largely run by the royal court. The government printed what it wanted spread: classics, histories, Buddhist and Confucian texts, often in small runs for officials and scholars. Gutenberg, by contrast, was a businessman working on borrowed money, and the printers who followed him had to sell books to survive, so they printed whatever buyers would pay for.
